<jats:p><div>
 The 2026 geopolitical environment marks a critical inflection point in global power dynamics. Traditional frameworks of conventional military and financial superiority are being offset by asymmetric leverage — decentralised, technology-enabled, and multi-stakeholder in nature. This memorandum presents a strategic roadmap for Regional Resilience and Financial Sovereignty across BRICS+ member states, grounded in three interlocking pillars: the doctrine of Technological Asymmetry in defence architecture; the transition to Currency Sovereignty through CBDC interoperability; and the 2026 geopolitical realignment of Gulf and Eastern Bloc financial relationships. The paper proposes the establishment of a BRICS Digital Currency Bridge (mBridge expansion) linking the e-Rupee, Digital Yuan, and Gulf-state CBDCs as a sovereign settlement ecosystem, bypassing USD-denominated infrastructure. It argues that India's BRICS 2026 Chairmanship represents a decisive window to formalise a Multipolar Financial Order.
</div></jats:p>
title: Asymmetric Resilience and the Transition to Multipolar Security Architecture: Focus on CBDC Interoperability for BRICS 2026

items.abstract:
<jats:p>Cross-border payments remain slower, costlier, and less transparent than domestic transactions due to long intermediation chains, fragmented messaging standards, prefunding requirements, FX spreads, and complex compliance checks. Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs), particularly in multi-CBDC (mCBDC) systems, are proposed as a way to shorten the value chain and enable new settlement designs such as atomic payment-versus-payment (PvP) FX settlement.
 
This chapter explores how CBDCs can transform cross-border payments through interoperability, programmability, and harmonized compliance frameworks. It reviews global pilot projects such as Project mBridge, Project Dunbar, and Project Helvetia, analyzes design choices for interoperability, and evaluates risks and recommendations for policymakers. The discussion highlights how mCBDC platforms can reduce costs, improve speed, enhance transparency, and strengthen financial integrity, while also introducing new challenges in governance, privacy, and geopolitics.</jats:p>
title: CROSS-BORDER CBDC & INTEROPERABILITY: CROSS-BORDER PAYMENTS & MULTIPLE CBDC SYSTEMS (MCBDC)
container-title: AI-Intelligence Driven Monetary Policy Optimization in CBDC Economies

items.abstract: <jats:p>Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs) are sovereign digital instruments designed to coexist with cash and reserves. Their success depends not only on design features but also on their ability to interoperate with existing financial infrastructure, including payment systems, clearing and settlement networks, banking platforms, and compliance frameworks. This chapter explores the technical, regulatory, and operational dimensions of CBDC interoperability, analyzing how integration with legacy systems can ensure efficiency, resilience, and adoption. It reviews global pilot projects, policy literature, and technical standards to highlight pathways for harmonization, while also identifying risks and offering recommendations for policymakers.</jats:p>
title: CBDC INTEROPERABILITY WITH EXISTING FINANCIAL INFRASTRUCTURE

items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper provides a comprehensive doctoral-level analysis of Project Dunbar-the landmark multi-central bank digital currency (mCBDC) experiment jointly conducted by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Innovation Hub, Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM), the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), and the South African Reserve al-Shariah and classical fiqh al-muamalat frameworks, and the extant literature on CBDC governance, this paper argues that Project Dunbar represents not merely a technical proof-ofconcept, but a geopolitical, monetary, and ethical inflection point for par ticipating nations. The paper concludes with a forward-looking policy framework for Malaysia and ASEAN, incorporating Islamic finance integration pathways, tokenised sukuk settlement mechanisms, and recommendations for a phased multi-CBDC governance architecture fit for a post-Bretton Woods multipolar monetary order.</jats:p>
title: Project Dunbar and the Future of Multi-CBDC Architecture

items.abstract:
<jats:p>Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs) are sovereign digital instruments designed to complement cash and reserves, offering new opportunities to enhance efficiency, resilience, and compliance in payment systems. Their architecture diverges into retail CBDCs, aimed at the general public for everyday transactions, and wholesale CBDCs, aimed at financial institutions for interbank settlement and cross-border efficiency.
 
This chapter provides a comprehensive analysis of both models, integrating global pilot evidence, regulatory frameworks, and policy literature. It examines design choices such as access models (direct vs. intermediated), identity frameworks (account-based vs. token-based), privacy thresholds, and offline functionality. The discussion highlights how retail CBDCs promote financial inclusion and consumer access, while wholesale CBDCs strengthen systemic stability and cross-border resilience.
 
The chapter also reviews compliance implications under AML, KYC, and CFT obligations, evaluates risks including privacy erosion, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, and regulatory fragmentation, and proposes recommendations for tiered access, privacy-by-design, interoperability, and alignment with global policy targets. By embedding programmable compliance and harmonized standards into CBDC architecture, central banks can transform both domestic and international payment systems, balancing efficiency with financial integrity.</jats:p>
title: CBDC DESIGN & ARCHITECTURE

items.abstract: <jats:p>A previous study clustered home occupants into archetypes with a questionnaire. This study uses qualitative methods to strengthen those previously-found archetypes with data pertaining to the participants’ home experiences. Focus groups were carried out where generative activities were conducted involving the generation of collages. The first activity dealt with the expression of ‘meaning of energy use at home’ and the second one with the ‘ideal home experience’. Analyses were done with content and thematic analysis. Codes were drawn from the data and were assimilated through an affinity diagram. The diagram produced two categories: building themes and human themes, along with five sub-categories (home, financial, energy, psychological, and behavioural aspects). The outcome shows that each archetype expresses needs and meanings of an ideal home experience and energy use differently from each other. The results provide evidence that generative techniques can be used in energy research. In this case, to validate and substantiate the quantitative archetypes previously produced with a questionnaire. Interpretive knowledge in energy research allows for a better understanding of occupants’ differing behavioural patterns in regards to energy use and comfort. It allows customizing interventions to the archetypes’ specific needs to decrease energy consumption while maintaining comfort.</jats:p>
title: Using focus groups data to finalize the Archetypes

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>A vendor agnostic design framework is proposed for multi‐terminal high voltage direct current (HVDC) here. An analytical assessment is then proposed as a first step of this assessment to quantify the domain of operating point. The criterion is indexed by the margin against loss‐of‐equilibrium for an Multi‐Vendor‐Multi‐Terminal (MVMT)‐HVDC network with terminal behaviour of connected converters. Based on a multi‐terminal control architecture, a static analytical model is established, including relevant parameters within the direct current network, its topology, and operation. Two types of scalar index are proposed and then normalized to indicate the margin against loss‐of‐equilibrium and then employed to quantify the domain of operating point. It is proposed that the domain of security shall correspond to a value in closer proximity to ‘1’ for better security. The effectiveness of the indices is verified and analysed with simulations in the environments of both Matlab/Simulink and real‐time digital simulator with pseudo‐steady‐state and detailed electro‐magnetic transient modelling, respectively. This approach attempts to represent one MVMT control scheme to support practical specification, testing and demonstration of the first MVMT‐HVDC control system as a business case.</jats:p>
title: Towards HVDC interoperability—Vendor agnostic control architecture and quantifying domain of operating point

items.abstract: <jats:p>Existing memory architectures for autonomous AI agents share a common design assumption: memory is a search problem. This assumption fails under the operational conditions of long-running agents serving specific entities over extended time horizons. An autonomous agent managing procurement, legal, and HR functions for a business across eighteen months does not need to search general knowledge. It needs to know what this specific entity did, what its connected systems reported, and what decisions were made-structured, compressed, and current at every session start. The same applies to a clinical AI agent serving a patient: it needs the patient's operational reality, not a semantic search over medical literature. Entity Continuous Awareness (ECA) introduces a model-agnostic, sector-agnostic operational context architecture for long-running autonomous agents. ECA defines the entity-a business, a patient, a legal case, a student-as the unit of context, and builds a continuously updated operational context layer from two sources: agent executions and connected external systems. ECA's four contributions are: (1) a five-layer temporal compression pyramid with an immutable_facts[] mechanism that preserves critical parameters through all compression cycles; (2) a delta recording protocol that captures structured operational events from both agent executions and connected systems automatically; (3) a hierarchical traversal protocol with link-based file forwarding that locates original artifacts and surfaces them as storage URLs without injecting file content into the session; and (4) fallback modes for temporal anchoring failure using BM25 full-text search and entity-graph lookup, with RAG reserved as last resort. ECA is an architectural specification, not currently deployed. It requires no specific AI model and applies to any sector where an entity has an operational history an agent must understand.</jats:p>
title: Entity Continuous Awareness (ECA): A Model-Agnostic, Sector-Agnostic Operational Context Architecture for Long-Running Autonomous Agents

items.abstract: <jats:p>Adversarial and evaluative reasoning systems share identical processing pathways. What differs across legal domains is vocabulary and output formatting, not reasoning. This paper formalizes that structural identity — essentialist convergence — and presents an architecture that exploits it: a three-layer system in which a universal reasoning engine operates on abstract entities, relationships, and signals; a swappable domain schema configures what those abstractions mean in a given practice area; and a domain-specific action layer translates conclusions into appropriate outputs. The reasoning engine processes information through three distinct modes — shape coherence, topographical weighting, and digital verification — operating in sequence from most fundamental to most specific. The architecture is demonstrated within California personal injury litigation (motor vehicle accidents) and designed with no domain-specific assumptions in the reasoning layer. A formal topographical model defines context as a coordinate vector, relevance as distance-to-frontier, and signal strength as a function of the case’s position in dimensional space rather than an intrinsic property of the evidence. The architecture’s resistance to hallucination is structural, not probabilistic: it distills downward through constraint rather than constructing upward through generation.</jats:p>
title: Essentialist Architecture for Domain-Agnostic Legal Reasoning

items.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">Although the adoption of distributed ledger technology (DLT) is still in a very early phase, its application to the issuance and custody of digital securities is making progress and various platforms and solutions based on a blockchain/DLT infrastructure are emerging. The cash leg of settlement, however, is still not properly solved for this type of infrastructure. For the settlement of digital assets, traditional payment rails are still often used, which hinders the technology from reaching its full potential in areas such as efficiency gains, both in respect of costs and time. To support and prepare for a potentially wider adoption of digital assets, the European Central Bank (ECB) is exploring in 2024 new technologies for wholesale central bank money settlement together with interested market participants. Central bank money systems have centralised architectures designed for single issuers and operators. As central bank money is traditionally used to support the settlement of securities, the question of how to bring it to newly emerging decentralised DLT platforms in an interoperable and efficient manner requires an answer. The ECB, together with three national banks as solution providers, is exploring three different approaches and will likely shed light on several important considerations: is wholesale central bank money necessary on-chain in a tokenised form? What are the advantages and disadvantages of alternative approaches? This paper provides a comparative overview of the explored solutions and describes the assumed interoperability mechanisms between the digital asset and payment systems.</jats:p>
title: Settlement of digital assets and wholesale CBDC : Solutions and interoperability approaches explored by the ECB

items.abstract: <jats:p>Urban population growth is estimated to exceed 50% by 2050 in today's urban spaces. Therefore, the mobility patterns of people and objects become a fundamental element for planning, control, and decision-making in multimodal transportation. The use of an agnostic system that allows us to obtain the best combination of technologies and cognitive predictive inference models covering all areas of transportation (road, maritime, and air) without programming language limitations, supported by probability distribution functions on the entropic maximization theory of complex stochastic systems as the core model that could be incorporated into a machine learning logical architecture. It allows for selecting the most efficient, harmonious, and sustainable transportation trajectory. The methodology employed is exploratory-descriptive and theoretical, based on experiences implemented in other countries, and the incorporation from the coupling of Shannon theory with Gamma distribution functions in multivariate stochastic systems for the transportation sector as an innovative contribution of this work. A representative model of an intelligent agnostic logical architecture is presented, where the integration of the multivariate system is shown, nourishing the argument in the justification of the use, and could be taken as a proposal to be developed and implemented to reduce road congestion, reduce environmental pollution, and provide a sustainable alternative. The challenge is the understanding of this intelligent agnostic system by legislators in the transport area for the implementation of “IoT” devices in each transport unit and routes for connectivity to a "brain" that receives information from other areas of transport and walkers from their devices with high-speed technology in data navigation</jats:p>
title: Justification of architecture for intelligent agnostic multimodal transportation

items.abstract: Since the 2025 Defence Capability Plan, New Zealand’s defence procurement framework requires every investment business case to begin by asking what Australia does. The framework stipulates interoperability with Five Eyes partners and discourages bespoke systems, yet the specific commercial platform choices through which that interoperability is achieved have received almost no public or parliamentary scrutiny. This article traces the emergence of a logic of interoperability through which alliance-mediated procurement routines come to normalise and entrench commercial platform dependency for small states. The empirical case explored here is New Zealand’s roughly fourteen-year integration with Palantir Technologies, with that investigation being further assisted by consideration of documentary evidence from the United Kingdom and a contrastive vignette from Switzerland. The paper argues that the logic of interoperability at play operates through a two-stage mechanism: anticipatory alignment narrows procurement options toward partner-compatible platforms before vendor selection, while infrastructural lock-in consolidates dependency through architecture, accreditation, training and exercise integration. Platform choices become progressively harder to revisit regardless of why they were initially made, raising questions about sovereignty and oversight that go beyond previous concerns about capability dependency and which demand closer scrutiny.
title: The Logic of Interoperability: Anticipatory Alignment, Infrastructural Lock-in and New Zealand’s Integration with Palantir
